Now there is a small difference between the true line-of-sight horizon and the optical horizon, but we're talking a maximum of a few miles. The thing is that air acts like a lense and therefore refracts light. On a flat Earth, objects at a distance would appear to float slightly in the air. In the real world, this effect allows us to see slightly over the true horizon under the right atmospheric conditions. Think of trying to view Chicago over Lake Michigan. It's not always possible because Chicago is just over the horizon. Sometimes you can only see the tops of the buildings. Sometimes you get a nice clear image. Sometimes the image is distorted or upside down. Sometimes you can't see it at all. It depends on the amount of moisture in the air and a few other atmospheric factors.
